$comment: Rule catalog — evaluation. Standards 2, 5, 6, 11, 12, 13, 18, 19, 20, 25. The largest category, and the one where automation helps least: whether a metric suits a problem, whether a period was cherry-picked, and whether a weak segment was omitted are all questions about what was not reported, and a repository contains only what was. One entry carries a detector. The rest are attestation-only, deliberately, per ADR 0004.

rules.title: A baseline exists and is reported beside the model
rules.description: A baseline is established before or alongside the first model, evaluated on the same data and split, and reported wherever the model's performance is reported.
rules.rationale: An improvement is a comparison, and a comparison needs something to compare against. A model reported without a baseline gives the reader no way to tell a real gain from a number that a constant predictor would have matched.
rules.remediation: Add the strongest simple thing that could reasonably work — a constant predictor, the current production rule, a linear model on the obvious features — evaluate it on the same split, and report it alongside.
rules.evidenceExpected: A baseline section or a baseline row in the results table of the evaluation document, showing the same metric on the same split.
rules.$assuranceNote: The check looks for a baseline heading or a baseline row in an evaluation document. A heading named Baseline is not an appropriate baseline: whether the comparison is fair, and whether the baseline is a strawman chosen because it is easy to beat, is the human question this standard actually asks.

rules.title: No improvement is claimed without an appropriate baseline
rules.description: An improvement must not be claimed unless a baseline appropriate to the problem was evaluated identically and the claim is stated relative to it. A baseline chosen because it is easy to beat does not satisfy this.
rules.rationale: A claim of improvement with no baseline, or with a strawman, is unfalsifiable in the direction that matters — the reader cannot tell whether the model beats doing nothing.
rules.remediation: State the baseline, its score, and the difference. Where the baseline was chosen for convenience, replace it with the strongest simple alternative and re-state the claim.
rules.evidenceExpected: An attestation that the baseline used for each improvement claim was the strongest reasonable simple alternative, not one selected for being beatable.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. Appropriateness of a baseline is a judgement about the problem, and the check that finds a baseline row cannot tell a serious one from a token one.

rules.title: Training performance is not reported as expected production performance
rules.description: A metric computed on data the model was fitted to must not be presented as an estimate of how the model will perform on data it has not seen.
rules.rationale: Training performance measures fit, not generalisation, and the gap between them is the entire reason held-out data exists. Reporting one as the other is the most common way an unusable model reaches a decision meeting looking finished.
rules.remediation: Report the held-out estimate as the performance figure, and label training performance as training performance wherever it appears.
rules.evidenceExpected: An attestation that each reported performance figure is labelled with the partition it was computed on.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. Which partition a number came from is not recoverable from the number.

rules.title: Evaluation periods are not selected after seeing the results
rules.description: The evaluation period must be chosen for its representativeness and fixed before results are seen. Selecting or trimming a window because of what it does to the reported figure is this prohibition.
rules.rationale: A favourable window produces a number that describes a period rather than a model, and the reader has no way to know which periods were tried.
rules.remediation: Fix the evaluation window in advance and report performance across all of it, including the periods that perform worst.
rules.evidenceExpected: An attestation naming when the evaluation period was fixed relative to the results, and stating what other windows, if any, were examined.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this, and it is undetectable by construction: the auditor cannot see the periods that were not reported. This is among the purest attestation cases in the framework.

rules.title: The class distribution is measured and accounted for
rules.description: Where classes are imbalanced, the base rate is measured and stated, the metric is chosen in light of it, and any resampling or weighting is applied to the training portion only and disclosed with its effect on the implied base rate.
rules.rationale: At a low base rate most metrics stop meaning what they appear to mean and most default thresholds stop being appropriate. Resampling also changes the base rate the model implies, which matters as soon as the output is read as a probability.
rules.remediation: State the class distribution beside the metric, choose a metric that survives it, and disclose any resampling along with what it does to the implied base rate.
rules.evidenceExpected: The measured class distribution recorded with the evaluation, and a disclosure of any resampling or weighting applied.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. The class distribution is a property of data the auditor does not read, so a check could not even tell whether the rule has a subject here.

rules.title: The metric follows from the problem and is fixed before the results
rules.description: The metric is derived from the problem, the cost of each kind of error, and the decision the output feeds, and is recorded before results that would tempt a different choice exist. Where several metrics are relevant, they are reported together.
rules.rationale: A metric chosen after the results is a metric chosen by the results. Fixing it in advance is what makes the eventual number evidence rather than a selection.
rules.remediation: Record the metric and the reasoning that produced it, referencing the cost asymmetry from the problem formulation, before running the evaluation that will be reported.
rules.evidenceExpected: A recorded metric choice with its justification, dated before the reported results, plus the set of metrics reported together where more than one is relevant.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. Whether accuracy suffices depends on the class distribution and the cost of an error, neither of which is visible in a repository — a scanner flagging a metric call would be guessing. Metrics found in code are reported descriptively and bound to no rule.

rules.title: Metrics are not selected for making the model look better
rules.description: A metric must not be chosen, swapped, or dropped because of what it does to the reported result. Reporting the subset of computed metrics that flatter the model is the same act as choosing one.
rules.rationale: Selecting the measure after seeing the measurements converts evaluation into presentation, and does so invisibly: the reported number is correctly computed, and it is the wrong number.
rules.remediation: Report every metric that was identified as relevant when the problem was formulated, including the ones that came out worse.
rules.evidenceExpected: An attestation that the reported metrics are the ones fixed in advance, and that no computed metric was dropped for being unflattering.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. The evidence would be a metric that was computed and not reported, which by definition is not in the report.

rules.title: Accuracy is not treated as sufficient for every problem
rules.description: Accuracy must not be used as the reported measure without establishing that it suits the problem's base rate and cost structure.
rules.rationale: At a low base rate a model that does nothing at all can post a high accuracy and beat a useful one. Accuracy as a default is not a neutral choice; it is a claim that the two kinds of error cost the same, made without anyone deciding it.
rules.remediation: Choose a metric that reflects the base rate and the cost asymmetry, and report accuracy only alongside it, if at all.
rules.evidenceExpected: A recorded justification that the reported metric suits the base rate and the cost of each error type.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. Flagging an accuracy call would require the class distribution and the cost of an error, and the auditor has neither.

rules.title: Calibration is measured where the output is used as a probability
rules.description: Where downstream decisions treat the output as a probability — thresholding on expected value, combining with costs, feeding another model — calibration is measured and reported, and recalibration is applied and disclosed where required.
rules.rationale: A score between zero and one is not a probability merely because it lies between zero and one. Any decision that multiplies the output by a cost is relying on calibration whether or not anyone measured it.
rules.remediation: Measure calibration on held-out data and report it, or stop describing the output as a probability and call it a score.
rules.evidenceExpected: A calibration measurement on held-out data, reported with the model, or a recorded determination that the output is not consumed as a probability.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. Verifying calibration requires running the model against data, which is outside a static auditor's contract.

rules.title: Confidence scores are not called probabilities without evidence
rules.description: A model output must not be described or consumed as a calibrated probability unless calibration has been measured. Absent that evidence, it is a score.
rules.rationale: Once an output is called a probability, downstream systems multiply it by costs and compare it across models. Every one of those uses is invalid if the number is merely ordered rather than calibrated, and none of them will fail loudly.
rules.remediation: Measure calibration, or rename the output and correct the downstream uses that assumed otherwise.
rules.evidenceExpected: An attestation that every place the output is described as a probability is backed by a calibration measurement.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. The word chosen in a downstream system's documentation is not in this repository, and the calibration measurement cannot be performed without running the model.

rules.title: Components are ablated to show what earns its place
rules.description: Where a model has separable components — engineered features, an architectural choice, an augmentation, a post-processing step — each is removed in turn and the model re-evaluated on the same data, split, and metric, and all arms are reported.
rules.rationale: A claim that the whole is good does not establish that each part contributes, and the usual finding is that a component can be removed with no loss — which is the more valuable result, because it simplifies the thing that has to be maintained.
rules.remediation: Run one ablation per separable component against the same split and metric, and report every arm including the ones that changed nothing.
rules.evidenceExpected: Ablation results covering each separable component, reported with the same metric and split as the headline comparison.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. An unreported ablation arm and an ablation never run leave the same trace, which is none.

rules.title: Models are not compared across different data or splits
rules.description: Two results must not be compared unless they were produced on the same data, the same split, the same metric, and the same preprocessing discipline. Where a difference in those conditions is intended, it is the experiment and must be declared as such.
rules.rationale: A difference in score between models evaluated on different data is not a difference between the models. The comparison reads as evidence and carries none.
rules.remediation: Re-evaluate the compared models under identical conditions, or state the differing condition as the variable under study.
rules.evidenceExpected: A recorded comparison protocol naming the shared dataset version, split, metric, and preprocessing, plus an attestation that every compared result used it.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. Whether two numbers came from the same split is a fact about how they were produced, and the repository holds only the numbers.

rules.title: Each claimed improvement is classified as statistical, practical, or production-relevant
rules.description: A claimed improvement states which of the three kinds it is — statistical, practically meaningful, production-relevant — and does not present one as another. A kind that was not assessed is stated as unassessed rather than assumed.
rules.rationale: The three are different claims with different evidence behind them, and a difference can be any combination of the three. Collapsing them lets a change that is real, tiny, and irrelevant to production be reported in the same words as one that matters.
rules.remediation: For each claimed improvement, say whether it is unlikely to be noise, whether it is large enough to change the decision it feeds, and whether it survives production conditions — naming any of the three that was not assessed.
rules.evidenceExpected: Comparison write-ups that classify each claimed improvement across the three kinds, with the evidence for each classification.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. Practical and production relevance depend on the decision the output feeds and on conditions the repository does not describe.

rules.title: A more complex model is not declared better on a slightly higher score
rules.description: A more complex model must not be selected over a simpler one on the strength of a small score difference alone. The difference must be shown to exceed the evaluation's noise and to be worth the complexity it buys.
rules.rationale: Complexity is paid for continuously — in latency, in maintenance, in the number of ways the thing can fail quietly — while a small score difference is often within the variance of the split. Selecting on the score alone systematically trades a durable cost for a difference that may not exist.
rules.remediation: Quantify the uncertainty around the difference, and state what the added complexity costs and what it buys, before selecting.
rules.evidenceExpected: An uncertainty estimate around the difference and a recorded justification for the added complexity.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. Model complexity has no repository-visible measure, and whether a difference is worth it is a judgement about operational cost.

rules.title: Comparisons carry an indication of uncertainty
rules.description: A comparison carries enough indication of uncertainty — a confidence interval, variance across folds or seeds, or a paired test — to tell a real difference from noise, and an unquantified difference is not described as an improvement.
rules.rationale: A single number hides how much it would move if the experiment were repeated. Without that, a difference and the noise around it are reported identically.
rules.remediation: Report variance across folds or seeds, or an interval around the difference, and match the method to the source of variation being estimated.
rules.evidenceExpected: An uncertainty estimate reported with each comparison, and the method used to produce it.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. Whether a reported interval was computed correctly, and whether it covers the variation that matters, are statistical judgements about work the repository records only as output.

rules.title: Segment-level performance is reported, including the weak segments
rules.description: Performance is broken down by the segments that matter for the model's use, and the breakdown accompanies the headline figure wherever it is reported.
rules.rationale: An aggregate metric routinely conceals a population for which the model does not work. A segment small in the data is not necessarily small in consequence, and the aggregate is the one number guaranteed not to show it.
rules.remediation: Add a segment breakdown to the evaluation and to the model card, choosing segments by who is affected rather than by what is convenient to compute.
rules.evidenceExpected: A segment-level results table in the evaluation document or model card, covering the segments identified as consequential.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. A check can see a table; it cannot see the segments that were not included in it.

rules.title: Poorly performing segments are not withheld
rules.description: A segment must not be omitted from reporting because the model performs badly on it. Where a segment cannot be reported for privacy or legal reasons, its existence and the reason for withholding it are still disclosed.
rules.rationale: The segments a model fails on are the ones its users most need to know about, and they are exactly the ones an author is least motivated to include. Omission leaves the reader unable to distinguish a segment that performs well from one that was never shown.
rules.remediation: Report every consequential segment. Where a breakdown genuinely cannot be published, say that it exists and why it is withheld.
rules.evidenceExpected: An attestation that the reported segments are all the consequential ones, naming any withheld and the reason.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this, and it is undetectable by construction: the auditor cannot see what was not reported. Alongside cherry-picked evaluation periods, this is the clearest case in the framework for attestation over automation.

rules.title: Reported performance states whether it was externally validated
rules.description: Reported performance states whether it was measured on data collected independently of the training data, and internal-holdout performance is not presented as if it established performance on a population the model was not evaluated on.
rules.rationale: A holdout is a partition of one collection, so it estimates performance on that collection soundly and carries no further on its own. Read without the qualifier it is taken for a transportability claim. TRIPOD and TRIPOD+AI treat external validation as a distinct study; Recht et al. (2019) rebuilt an ImageNet test set by the original protocol and accuracy fell across every model examined.
rules.remediation: State beside the reported figures which collection they were measured on, and whether any evaluation population was collected independently of the development data — a different site, population, or period, not a partition of the same collection. 'Not externally validated' is a complete answer; a split drawn on an arbitrary column and called an external population is not.
rules.evidenceExpected: A statement accompanying the reported performance that names the collection it was measured on and says whether an independently collected evaluation population exists, with its provenance where one does.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated establishes this. Whether two datasets were collected independently is a fact about their origin, not about the repository, and no detector can see it. A scan cannot even establish which reported figure came from which partition.
